newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Falklands oil plan deadline requires more effort.
newsitem.headline: Falklands oil plan deadline requires more effort.

text.p: Britain and Argentina will have to work harder to reach their year-end deadline for a joint round of oil licensing off the disputed Falkland Islands, officials at bilateral talks said on Wednesday.

After three days of talks on oil exploration around the South Atlantic islands, where Britain and Argentina fought a war in 1982, the two countries confirmed their interest in tendering oil permits for a "Special Cooperation Zone" southwest of the Falklands.

However, the two-nation South West Atlantic Hydrocarbons Commission said in a joint press statement that "work would have to be intensified to realise this objective" -- set in London last December when the timetable was also agreed.
"Priority should be given to work on detailed terms and conditions under which licenses will be issued in the Special Cooperation Area," said the statement.

The government of the remote British-run islands awarded permits for exploration in waters close to the islands to 12 firms in October. The new licenses are for an area straddling the line between the islands and the Argentine mainland.

Under the complex agreement on oil and gas exploration signed in 1995, both countries can levy royalties on any oil discovered -- the Falklands at nine percent and Argentina at three percent -- without recognising each other's right to levy the charge.
The negotiations take place under a so-called "diplomatic umbrella" by which both sides agree to put aside sovereignty claims and tackle specific issues such as oil and fishing.
Argentina lost the 1982 war for the islands it calls the Malvinas but continues to press its 150-year-old territorial claim. The two former foes resumed diplomatic links in 1989.

Britain and Argentina pledged to carry out a survey of the marine environment in the area where oil licences will be sold and scientific research, as well as the detection and tracking of floating icebergs.
